text: Hello?
Take a deep breath.
Stop scrolling for a second.
I want you to close your eyes and think back to when you were seven years old.
Do you remember the summer holidays, specifically the summer of your childhood?
Think about how long they felt.
Those six weeks away from school felt like an entire lifetime.
You could wake up, watch cartoons, build a fortress in the garden, have a war with
your friends, learn to ride a bike, and explore the woods all before lunchtime.
The days stretched out into the horizon.
The sun seemed to hang in the sky forever.
A single afternoon could hold a thousand adventures.
Back then time was not something you measured.
It was something you lived in.
It felt infinite.
It felt like you would be young forever.
But then something happened.
You grew up.
You hit 20, then 25, then 30.
Suddenly you blink and it is Monday again.
You blink again and it is Christmas.
You blink one more time and you're blowing out candles on a cake with a number you do
not recognize.
You look at photos from five years ago and it feels like yesterday.
You ask yourself, where did the time go?
This is not just a feeling.
This is a universal human experience.
It is called the time paradox and it is terrifying because if it keeps speeding up like this,
the next 10 years will feel like five and the 10 years after that will feel like two.
Why does this happen?
Is the universe playing a cruel trick on us?
Actually, the answer lies in simple mathematics.
In 1897 the French philosopher Paul Janet proposed a theory.
It is called the proportional theory.
Let's break it down.
Imagine you are five years old.
To a five year old, one year is a massive amount of time.
Mathematically, one year represents 20% of your entire existence.
Think about that.
One fifth of everything you have ever known is just one single year.
That is why waiting for your next birthday felt like torture.
It was a huge percentage of your history.
Now, fast forward, you are 50 years old.
One year now represents only 2% of your life.
Just 2% to your brain that year is just a tiny, insignificant drop in the ocean of memories
you have already stored.
As we age, each unit of time becomes a smaller fraction of our life experience.
We perceive time logarithmically, not linearly.
This is why your childhood felt like a slow motion movie and your adulthood feels like
a video on fast forward.
But math is only the beginning.
If it was just math, we could not do anything about it.
But we can, because the real reason is much deeper.
It is happening inside your skull right now.
Let's talk about neuroscience.
Your brain is not just a clock.
It is a complex machine designed for survival.
And more importantly, it is a machine designed for efficiency.
Think of your brain as a video camera that records your life onto a hard drive.
But this camera does not record at a steady speed.
It has a variable frame rate.
When you are a child, your brain is developing rapidly.
Your neural networks are exploding with connections.
The world is full of firsts.
The first time you saw the ocean, the first time you tasted ice cream, the first time
you felt the sting of a bee, the first heartbreak.
Because everything is new, your brain is in a state of hyper-awareness.
It pays attention to everything.
It records every detail, the smell of the saltwater, the cold texture of the ice cream, the sound
of the bee.
It is recording at 60 frames per second.
High definition, 4K resolution.
Because there is so much data being written onto your memory hard drive.
When you look back, the file size is huge.
The memory feels long.
But as we enter adulthood, the firsts stop happening.
We settle into.
The routine.
You wake up at the same time.
You brush your teeth with the same hand.
You drive the same route to work.
You sit in the same chair.
You talk to the same colleagues about the same problems.
You eat the same sandwich.
You watch the same type of TV shows.
Your brain is smart.
It realizes, wait a minute.
I have seen this movie before.
I know this route.
I know this taste.
So to save energy, it stops recording.
It switches from 60 frames per second.
Down to 15.
It stops writing new data.
It just references the old data.
It goes into auto pilot mode.
Have you ever driven home from work, parked your car, and suddenly realized you remember
absolutely nothing about the drive?
You don't remember the traffic lights.
You don't remember the songs on the radio.
You don't remember turning the steering wheel.
That is the eraser of routine.
Your brain literally deleted that hour of your life because nothing new happened.
You compress the data.
Now imagine living your whole life like that drive home.
Monday becomes Tuesday.
Tuesday becomes Friday.
January becomes December.
When your brain compresses days into hours and months into weeks, life begins to blur.
This is why you can remember a one week vacation to a foreign country more vividly than an
entire year of sitting in your office.
The vacation was full of new data.
The office was just a loop.
This is the tragedy of the modern adult.
We trade novelty for comfort.
We trade adventure for security.
And the price we pay for that comfort is time.
So is this our fate?
Are we doomed to watch the clock spin faster and faster until we run out of time?
Are we just passengers on a high speed train watching the scenery blur into a gray smear?
No.
There's a way to slow it down.
We cannot stop the physics of time, but we can hack our perception of it.
We can trick our brain into recording at 60 frames per second again.
The secret is not magic.
The secret is novelty.
You need to wake up your brain.
You need to force it to pay attention.
And no, you do not need to quit your job and travel the world to do this.
You can do it right here today in your ordinary life.
Not small.
If you usually drive to work, take the bus tomorrow or drive a different route, even if
it takes 10 minutes longer.
Those 10 minutes will be remembered because your brain has to navigate new streets.
If you usually eat lunch at your desk, go outside.
Feel the wind.
Look at the sky.
Read a book about a subject you know nothing about.
Listen to a genre of music you usually hate.
You have to arrange the furniture in your bedroom.
Brush your teeth with your left hand.
It sounds silly, I know, but these small shocks to the system force your brain to exit
autopilot mode.
They create new neural pathways.
They create new frames in your movie.
By introducing newness, you are literally stretching your time.
The stoic philosopher Seneca once wrote a book called, on the shortness of life.
He said,
Life is not short.
We just waste a lot of it.
We waste it on anxiety.
We waste it on anger.
We waste it on mindless scrolling.
But mostly we waste it on being asleep while we are awake.
So here is my challenge to you.
Do not let your life become a blurry commute between Monday and Friday.
Do not let this year look exactly like last year.
Seek out the uncomfortable.
Seek out the new.
Be curious.
Be present.
Look at the person you love.
Really look at them.
Notice the lines on their face.
Listen to their voice.
Taste your coffee.
Feel the warmth of the cup.
Because in the end, time is the only currency you truly have.
You cannot save it.
You cannot buy more of it.
You can only spend it.
So spend it on things worth remembering.
Slow down.
Look around and stay curious.
Thanks for stopping by.
